title: Micro Frontends
description: Architecture patterns for scalable frontend teams.

data.text: Micro frontends extend microservice principles to frontend development, allowing teams to ship features independently.

data.caption: Micro frontend teams composing a shell app

data.text: A Shell That Loads a Remote at Runtime

Runtime composition loads each team's bundle from its own deployment. In Module Federation the shell declares remotes by URL, and a remote exposes a component entry point. Because the remote is fetched at runtime, the shell can pick up a new version without being redeployed — but a failed remote must be handled with a boundary so the rest of the page still renders.

data.title: Shell consuming a remote module

data.text: Once several bundles run in one page they share global scope, and that is where micro frontends hurt. Two teams can register the same global, load two versions of React, or ship conflicting CSS selectors. The mitigations are real: decide whether the shell or each remote owns the framework, scope CSS with modules or shadow DOM, and make the boundary between shell and remote an explicit, versioned contract.

data.title: Sharing a framework singleton
Interview angle: when micro frontends are the wrong answer
data.text: Micro frontends solve an organizational problem — several teams shipping one app without coordinating releases — at the cost of runtime composition, duplicated dependencies, and boundaries that are harder to debug. A single team building a single product will get more value from a modular monolith: one build, one framework version, shared code without network boundaries. Say that the decision is driven by team topology, not by technical preference, and that a shared design system and a monorepo usually come first.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Micro frontends scale teams and deployments.
